title: Principal Weil divisor map of a normal Noetherian domain and its kernel of units
statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative Noetherian normal domain [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring, def-weil-pbc-normal-ring], where domain means $1\ne0$ and no zero divisors, and identify $R$ with its image in the fraction field $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$. Let $H$ be its height-one primes: the nonzero prime ideals $\mathfrak q$ having no prime strictly between $(0)$ and $\mathfrak q$. The localization $R_{\mathfrak q}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] is a discrete valuation ring [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring] for every $\mathfrak q\in H$. Write $v_{\mathfrak q}:K^\times\to\mathbf Z$ for its normalized additive valuation, characterized by $v_{\mathfrak q}(u\pi^e)=e$ for a local unit $u$, a uniformizer $\pi$, and $e\in\mathbf Z$. For $x\in K^\times$, membership in $R_{\mathfrak q}$ is equivalent to $v_{\mathfrak q}(x)\geq0$, and membership in $R_{\mathfrak q}^\times$ is equivalent to $v_{\mathfrak q}(x)=0$. For every $x\in K^\times$ the set $\{\mathfrak q\in H:v_{\mathfrak q}(x)\ne0\}$ is finite, and these values agree with the length-difference orders defining affine Weil divisors [def-trf-affine-weil-divisor-class-group]. Consequently the formula
$$\operatorname{div}_R(x)=\sum_{\mathfrak q\in H}v_{\mathfrak q}(x)[\mathfrak q]$$
defines a homomorphism from the multiplicative group $K^\times$ to the additive group $\operatorname{Div}(R)=\bigoplus_{\mathfrak q\in H}\mathbf Z[\mathfrak q]$: $\operatorname{div}_R(xy)=\operatorname{div}_R(x)+\operatorname{div}_R(y)$. Its kernel is exactly the image of $R^\times\to K^\times$:
$$\operatorname{div}_R(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in R^\times.$$
This includes a field $R$, when $H$ is empty and $\operatorname{Div}(R)=0$.

source.place: Tags 00PD (lemma-characterize-dvr), 031S (lemma-criterion-normal), 031T (lemma-normal-domain-intersection-localizations-height-1), together with divisors.tex Tags 02RL (lemma-divisor-locally-finite), 0BE3 (definition-principal-divisor), 02RP (lemma-div-additive). proof.text: Fix a height-one prime $\mathfrak q$ and put $B=R_{\mathfrak q}$. Localization preserves Noetherianity and normality, and embeds $B$ in $K$ with fraction field $K$, by the two localization lemmas. Its dimension is one by the localization dimension lemma: in a domain the primes below $\mathfrak q$ form precisely the chain $(0)\subsetneq\mathfrak q$. It is local by the definition of prime localization. Thus the normal one-dimensional local-domain lemma makes $B$ a DVR. In particular its maximal ideal is generated by a nonzero nonunit $\pi$.

In each $B$, the unit-times-uniformizer-power lemma writes each nonzero $a\in B$ as $u\pi^n$ with $n\ge0$. The exponent is unique: equality of two such expressions with unequal exponents would, after cancellation, make a positive power of the nonunit $\pi$ a unit. For $x=a/b\in K^\times$, define $v(x)=n(a)-n(b)$. If $a/b=c/d$, then $ad=bc$; multiplying the power expressions and using uniqueness gives $n(a)+n(d)=n(b)+n(c)$, so $v$ is well defined. The same multiplication gives $v(xy)=v(x)+v(y)$ and the expression $x=u\pi^{v(x)}$ with $u\in B^\times$. These formulas give $v(\pi)=1$ and characterize $v$ uniquely, independently of the chosen uniformizer, since any two generators differ by a unit. If $x\in B$ then $v(x)\ge0$; conversely the displayed expression puts $x$ in $B$ when $v(x)\ge0$. Finally $x\in B^\times$ implies both $v(x)$ and $-v(x)=v(x^{-1})$ are nonnegative, hence $v(x)=0$; the converse follows from $x=u\pi^0$. This constructs exactly the normalized valuations and both membership criteria in the statement. For completeness, if $x+y\ne0$, put $m=\min(v(x),v(y))$. Then $\pi^{-m}x$ and $\pi^{-m}y$ lie in $B$, so their nonzero sum lies in $B$; multiplicativity and the membership criterion give $v(x+y)\ge m$. Thus these maps satisfy the valuation inequality as well.

source.place: Tag 00PD (lemma-characterize-dvr), final assertion and proof constructing v(a/b)

proof.text: For $a=u\pi^n\ne0$ in $B$, the ideal $aB$ equals $\pi^nB$. The residue field $B/\pi B$ has length one by the definition of module length: its only $B$-submodules are zero and itself. For $n\ge0$ there is a short exact sequence $0\to B/\pi^nB\xrightarrow{\cdot\pi}B/\pi^{n+1}B\to B/\pi B\to0$; injectivity follows by cancellation of $\pi$, and the kernel of reduction is its image. Additivity of length and induction from $B/B=0$ give $\operatorname{length}_B(B/\pi^nB)=n$. Therefore $\operatorname{length}_B(B/aB)=v(a)$, always finite. For nonzero $a,b\in R$, the length-difference order of $a/b$ is consequently $v(a)-v(b)=v(a/b)$, exactly the order in the affine Weil-divisor definition. The length comparison has thus been proved, rather than taken from the explanatory sentence in that definition.

source.place: Tags 02LY (definition-length), 00IV (lemma-length-additive), 02MD (definition-ord); applied to the DVR supplied by 00PD

proof.text: Write $x=a/b$ with $a,b\in R$ nonzero. If neither $a$ nor $b$ belongs to $\mathfrak q$, their inverses belong to $R_{\mathfrak q}$ by the fraction definition, so both are local units and $v_{\mathfrak q}(x)=0$. Thus the support is contained in the union of the height-one primes containing $a$ or $b$. Any height-one prime containing the nonzero $a$ is minimal over $(a)$: a strictly smaller prime would be $(0)$, which cannot contain $a$. The same applies to $b$. The finite-minimal-primes lemma, applied to $(a)$ and $(b)$ in the Noetherian ring $R$, therefore gives finite support.

source.place: Tag 00FR (lemma-Noetherian-irreducible-components), applied to principal-ideal quotients; affine denominator version of divisors.tex Tag 02RL (lemma-divisor-locally-finite)

proof.text: By finite support the function $\mathfrak q\mapsto v_{\mathfrak q}(x)$ is an element of the direct sum $\operatorname{Div}(R)$ of the affine Weil-divisor definition. Equality of such functions is coordinatewise. The multiplicativity formula of Step 2 gives $\operatorname{div}_R(xy)=\operatorname{div}_R(x)+\operatorname{div}_R(y)$ and $\operatorname{div}_R(1)=0$, so this is the claimed homomorphism. Step 3 identifies it with the length-difference principal divisor.

We prove the intersection assertion needed for the kernel, following the proof of Tag 031T(2). Suppose $z=b/a\in K$ with $a\ne0$ belongs to every height-one localization. Apply the principal-quotient associated-height lemma to $R/aR$: each of its associated primes $\mathfrak p$ has height one. For each such $\mathfrak p$, membership $b/a\in R_{\mathfrak p}$ means $b/a=c/s$ for some $c\in R$ and $s\notin\mathfrak p$. Equality in $K$ gives $sb=ac$ in $R$, since $R\hookrightarrow K$ is injective. Hence $s$ annihilates the class $\bar b$ in $R/aR$. The equivalent annihilator criterion in the module-injection lemma now gives $\bar b=0$, so $b=ar$ for some $r\in R$ and $z=r\in R$. The converse inclusion is immediate from $r=r/1$. This also works when there are no associated primes: the same injection criterion then forces $R/aR=0$.

source.place: Tag 031T (lemma-normal-domain-intersection-localizations-height-1), clauses (1),(2) and proof of (2); Tag 0311 (lemma-zero-at-ass-zero)

proof.text: If $\operatorname{div}_R(x)=0$, each valuation is zero, so Step 2 puts both $x$ and $x^{-1}$ in every height-one localization. Step 6 puts both in $R$. Their product is $1$ in $K$, hence also in $R$ by injectivity, so $x\in R^\times$. Conversely a unit of $R$ and its inverse belong to every localization, hence have valuation zero by Step 2; its divisor vanishes. These inclusions identify the kernel with the image of $R^\times\to K^\times$.

source.place: Tag 031T (lemma-normal-domain-intersection-localizations-height-1), clause (2), and Tag 00PD (lemma-characterize-dvr), valuation description

proof.text: If $R$ is a field there are no nonzero prime ideals, so $H$ is empty and the group of finitely supported functions on $H$ is zero. Also $K=R$ and every nonzero element is a unit. The constructed map is the zero map and its kernel is all of $K^\times=R^\times$, as required.
